🔹 It was necessary for Adel to be filtered! A successful program based on the personal abilities of Adel Ferdowsipour and the excitement of a popular and controversial game becomes the most-watched media program, compensating for part of the media's inability to connect with its viewers, but ultimately it is condemned to death by the management of a newly arrived manager. The host, using his ability and intelligence, sets up a private internet platform, and its audience soon surpasses that of the national media. But this is no longer tolerated. Adel's website is filtered. Using football examples to describe many social problems is useful because people easily relate to football. Personally, in this channel, I have used it many times to model the country's problems; I have listed some of them below. (I was surprised myself by the length of the list.) People know that success on the football field is not possible without proper planning and management, and only with luck and slogans. They know you can't win when you are weaker. They know that when their team loses, someone is definitely at fault: the Ministry of Sports, the Federation, the club, the coach, the players, or at least the referee, maybe all of them. They understand that without proper management and planning, it can't, it can't, it can't, no, it won't work. Maybe that's why a critical program about football is not tolerated. Even though it doesn't talk about politics and governance, it becomes a mirror reflecting management events across the whole country. People can easily find similarities in decision-making errors. Adel had to be filtered so that the large crowd supporting his programs, regardless of their team colors or political leanings, would become familiar with the country's most important management problem: arbitrary management, family management, rent-seeking management, unaccountable management, and ultimately, easy management. entry.title: 🔹 When ignorant fools are seated at the table In a series of behavioral…
entry.summary:
Source: @RezaEjtehadi

🔹 When ignorant fools are seated at the table In a series of behavioral experiments and animal intelligence tests, an animal—be it a rat, dolphin, or bird—is kept in a cage and must perform a task desired by the experimenter to receive a reward. For example, it must press a lever to open a hatch and receive some food, and repeat this for more food. Intelligent animals eventually learn how to get food. A more complex form of these experiments is when the lever and the food source are far apart. The animal must perform an action on one side of the cage and receive the reward on the other. Obviously, discovering this secret requires more intelligence. In a series of experiments first conducted with pigs in the late 1970s*, later known in game theory as the "Pig Game" (Boxed Pigs), two pigs are placed in a cage simultaneously. Now suppose that in this game's design, the distance between the lever and the food is very large, and also suppose that the two pigs differ in intelligence. The smarter pig eventually figures out how to get the food and presses the lever. But by the time it reaches the food source, a large portion has been eaten by the stupid pig, leaving little for it. There is no hope for the stupid pig, so it goes all the way again to press the lever, and the same story repeats. The stupid pig doesn't even need to think about where the food comes from. It sits there waiting for a hand from the unseen to pour some food. The continuation of this story turns the smart pig into a slave, constantly striving and moving from one side of the cage to the other to provide food, and the stupid pig into a pampered, lazy master. https://t.me/RezaEjtehadi ------------------ * Baldwin and Meese (1979)

entry.title: 🔹 The Powerless Powerful You wake up in the morning, start the usual routine…
entry.summary:
Source: @RezaEjtehadi

🔹 The Powerless Powerful You wake up in the morning, start the usual routine of another day of life. After the bathroom and possibly a morning shower, you go to prepare tea and open the fridge for breakfast. No need to think; the same breakfast as always. Woe to the day when one of the breakfast components has run out and you forgot to buy it. What disaster is greater than this? As you get older, you become more dependent on daily routines. When you are young, you quickly replace bread and cheese with an omelet or fried eggs. You might even call a friend to go out for breakfast. But as you age, changing life routines becomes harder and harder. Because change requires "decision," and what a difficult task that is. The bigger the decision, the harder it becomes, and one of the hardest decisions is the decision to retire. To accept that enough is enough. A decision that changes the entire life plan. Perhaps at 60 you might have the courage to retire voluntarily, but if you pass 80, it becomes impossible. You will no longer have the ability to make such a decision. So if you are still in a position or office after 80, it is not due to your ability, but your inability to decide. https://t.me/RezaEjtehadi

🔹 If you don't reform, you will break Metals are malleable. That is, they can be reshaped by hammer blows. With each blow, a slight change occurs, and eventually, they take shape according to need and use. But glass or ceramics cannot tolerate deformation. They resist blows, and if the blow is heavy, they break. Malleable iron, with a little impurity, becomes brittle cast iron. Cast iron has no way to change shape except by breaking or melting it. A government that no pressure can cause even a particle of change in its policy. It sits at the center of pressure and maintains its shape until the moment before it breaks. If you think you are very strong and stable, you yourself are the cause of breaking. https://t.me/RezaEjtehadi

entry.title: #BookExcerpt Taken from "The Selfish Gene" by Richard Dawkins. This book…
entry.summary:
Source: @RezaEjtehadi

#BookExcerpt Taken from "The Selfish Gene" by Richard Dawkins. This book presents Darwin's theory in simple language, focusing on the gene rather than the organism. Perhaps if I hadn't given this explanation, a reader unfamiliar with the author and book might think, after reading a few lines below, that it was a book about political science, war, or international competition: "The general answer to this question is that belligerence, besides its benefits, also has costs, apart from the obvious costs of time and energy. For example, suppose B and C are both my rivals, and I happen to confront B. Perhaps it would be reasonable for me, as a selfish individual, to try to eliminate him. But wait. C is both my rival and B's rival. By killing B, I actually benefit C as well, removing one of his rivals. Perhaps it would be better for me to let B live, because he might engage in competition with C, which would indirectly benefit me. The moral conclusion of this simple hypothetical example is that there is no obvious advantage in unthinkingly trying to kill rivals. In a large and complex competitive system, eliminating a rival is not necessarily beneficial; other rivals may benefit more from that killing than the individual himself." https://t.me/RezaEjtehadi

🔹 We are no less than the soil
"How does the soil breathe? Let us think...
Birds of the air died in flocks
The flower-bringers of the eternal meadow withered
In the sky and on the earth, ambush had panicked
In the narrowness of time, death had lingered!
Has the world come to an end?
The sky had no answer
Will the garden laugh again?
No one was certain
What a strange bitter cold...
How does the soil breathe? Let us learn: the glory of sprouting, now:
The dawn of Farvardin!
All that snow melted
All these flowers bloomed
All these colors blossomed!
The earth taught us
Not to step back before the event
Are we less than the soil?
The earth breathed
Why should we not breathe?"
Excerpt from the poem "How Does the Soil Breathe" by the late Fereydoun Moshiri, from the collection "Eternal Beauty"
